tone_statements.citation: Sapir, Edward (1922). The Takelma Language of Southwestern Oregon. In Handbook of American Indian languages: Volume 2. Washington: Government Printing Office. pp. 1-296.
tone_statements.quote: As in many Indian languages, the stress-accent of any particular word in Takelma is not so inseparably associated with any particular syllable but that the same word, especially if consisting of more than two syllables, may appear with the main stress-accent now on one, now on the other syllable. [...] Nevertheless a fully accented word is normally stressed on some particular syllable; it may even happen that two forms differ merely in the place of accent: naga'-ida when he said, but naga-ida' when you said. The important point to observe, however, is that when a particular syllable does receive the stress (and after all most words are normally accented on some one syllable), it takes on one of two or three musical inflections: (1) A simple pitch distinctly higher than the normal pitch of unstressed speech. (2) A rising inflection that starts at, or a trifle above, the normal pitch, and gradually slides up to the same higher pitch referred to above. (3) A falling inflection that starts at, or generally somewhat higher than, the raised pitch of (1) and (2), and gradually slides down to fall either in the same or immediately following syllable, to a pitch somewhat lower than the norm

readall_conflicts: No disagreement among what was opened for this item, because the single listed work (Golla 2011) yielded nothing: the copy consulted is front matter only. One labelling tension worth noting for the catalog: the catalog records Takelma as 'tonal' with an empty rule, whereas the primary description already held by the project in our files (Sapir 1922 / Collected Works VIII, §5 'Stress and pitch accent', BAE Bull. 40 pp. 15-16 = CW VIII pp. 31-32; downloaded 2026-09-16 by an earlier reading, NOT a listed work here) describes a mobile stress-accent -- "the stress-accent of any particular word in Takelma is not so inseparably associated with any particular syllable but that the same word, especially if consisting of more than two syllables, may appear with the main stress-accent now on one, now on the other syllable" -- whose stressed syllable "takes on one of two or three musical inflections" (raised, rising, falling pitch). That is a stress-plus-pitch accent system rather than lexical tone in the usual sense, so 'tonal' with no stress statement undersells it; Golla's §4.3 title 'Pitch Accent and Tone' (p. 209) suggests he treats it under the same heading, but the page itself was not available to check.

audit.reasoning: The classification (tonal / pitch accent, no positional stress rule, accent placement lexical-grammatical with minimal pairs by place of accent and by pitch contour) rests on Sapir's 296-page reference grammar, the only first-hand description of this extinct isolate, and every quoted passage and locator was confirmed in the full text we hold (pp. 15-16, 20, 55, 283). Glottolog's descriptive bibliography contains nothing on Takelma phonology beyond Sapir and its 1990 reprint, which I downloaded (open archive.org text) and which confirms the passages and documents that no later fieldwork exists. The one refinement available in the literature is Sapir's own 1936 phonemicization (reported in the downloaded volume via Hymes/Shipley, and presumably in Golla 2011): the raised and rising 'inflections' are length-conditioned variants, leaving a two-way pitch contrast on a freely placed accent. sources.quote: Texts key: falling accent = fall in pitch of stressed vowel; raised accent 'found on short vowels or unitonal long vowels ...
